rationale: A wins because it turns the same facts into four actual newsroom routes and shows what would kill each one. Its strongest move is “Calm has 4 million paying subscribers. Its insurer deal hands the app free to 25 million,” which finds the business-model tension B wrongly refuses as “Business/revenue mechanics — no_journalist_shape.” B has usable bones, but “The Wellness-to-Clinical Shift Is Arriving” and “Coverage Was the Last Wall” outkick the supplied facts and start sounding like a conference panel title.
gaps_in_A: “pointing to a randomized trial as the reason” slightly overstates the update; the facts say the deal and study exist, not that insurers relied on the study.
The member-service angle needs insurer names and activation steps before it is pitchable; A says this, but the headline “Your health plan may now include Calm Premium” is still soft without them.
A could separate “covered benefit” from “wellness add-on” even earlier, because that distinction can change the whole payer story.
gaps_in_B: “The Wellness-to-Clinical Shift Is Arriving” invents a clinical-threshold frame the update does not prove. A covered app benefit is not automatically a clinical product story.
“Coverage Was the Last Wall” is unsupported drama. The update gives a 25 million-member distribution deal, not proof that coverage was the final barrier to mental-health access.

“The prevailing belief in tech-health press is that independent university execution neutralizes industry funding” is an invented straw man unless you bring outside evidence, which this exercise does not allow.
Refusing “Business/revenue mechanics — no_journalist_shape” is the bad call. The 4 million paid subscribers versus 25 million no-cost covered members is exactly the business question.
